title: AI Inference Semiconductor Demand in APAC: What the Data Shows
summary: AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC analysed with hard data: GPU vs custom silicon costs, deployment patterns, power constraints and what it means for operators.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** APAC's AI inference semiconductor demand is growing faster than the region can power it. Taiwan holds ~90% of sub-10nm logic capacity, but the binding constraint for deploying companies is megawatts and per-token serving cost — not wafer supply.

# AI Inference Semiconductor Demand in APAC: Why the Real Story Is Consumption, Not Supply


Most coverage of AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC treats the region as a supplier — fabs, packaging, export tonnage. That framing is a decade out of date. The more interesting number is on the demand side: APAC is becoming one of the largest *consumers* of inference silicon, and the binding constraint for companies deploying here is not wafer supply. It's megawatts, rack space, and the per-token cost of serving a model to a customer in Jakarta at 9pm. Understanding AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC today means looking past fab headlines and into deployment economics.

Training gets the headlines because it's lumpy and expensive. Inference is the line item that compounds. Every query, every product recommendation, every support ticket summarised — that's a recurring compute cost that scales with your customer base, not with your R&D budget. For operators running teams across Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and Australia, that distinction changes which chips you should care about and where you should put them.


Here's what the data actually says.


## Inference is where the recurring spend sits, and the mix is shifting fast


Global semiconductor sales hit USD 627.6 billion in 2024, up 19.1% year on year, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association. The Asia Pacific/All Other region remained the largest single market by sales destination. WSTS, whose forecasts the SIA publishes, has pointed to continued double-digit growth into 2026 driven almost entirely by logic and memory tied to AI workloads.


The clearest single indicator of the training-to-inference shift is TSMC's revenue mix. High performance computing accounted for the majority of TSMC's quarterly revenue through 2025 — crossing well past the 50% mark and overtaking smartphones as the company's anchor platform (TSMC investor relations). That's a structural change in what Taiwan's capacity is pointed at, and a leading indicator for AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC more broadly.


On the buy side, NVIDIA's data centre segment passed USD 41 billion in a single quarter (Q2 FY2026, NVIDIA investor relations). A growing share of that is inference rather than training — NVIDIA's own commentary has repeatedly flagged inference as the faster-growing portion of data centre demand as reasoning models multiply token generation per query. According to TrendForce's 2025 market analysis, inference workloads are expected to account for the majority of AI accelerator shipment volume in the region within the next two years, a sharp reversal from the training-dominated buildout of 2023 and 2024.


The operational read: if your AI spend profile looks like a one-off capex item, you're early. Within 18 months it looks like a utility bill.


## Taiwan and Korea make the chips; Southeast Asia is now buying the capacity


Taiwan concentrates the overwhelming majority of leading-edge logic capacity — estimates from TrendForce and industry analysts consistently put Taiwan's share of sub-10nm foundry capacity around 90%. Korea dominates high-bandwidth memory, with SK hynix and Samsung together holding effectively the entire HBM market by revenue (TrendForce).


But deployment is moving south and west. Three data points worth holding together:


- Singapore's Green Data Centre Roadmap, published by IMDA, committed to at least 300MW of additional capacity in the near term with further headroom via green energy deployments — after a multi-year moratorium.
- Johor, Malaysia has absorbed a large share of the overflow, with Southeast Asia ranking as one of the fastest-growing data centre development markets globally, according to Cushman & Wakefield's 2025 report on the region.
- Japan has put state backing behind Rapidus, which began 2nm pilot line operation in 2025 with mass production targeted for 2027 (Rapidus corporate disclosures).


So the geography of APAC inference splits: fabrication clusters in Northeast Asia, deployment capacity in Southeast Asia, and demand distributed everywhere. This split is precisely why AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC can't be measured by fab output alone — consumption and production are increasingly decoupled.


For a company headquartered in London or New York, that split is an advantage, not a complication. You can serve Asian customers from Singapore or Johor with latency under 30ms to most of ASEAN, procure silicon through the same hyperscaler contracts you already hold, and staff the operations layer out of Hong Kong, Taipei or Manila.

## GPU versus custom silicon: the price-performance gap is real but conditional


This is where most procurement decisions go wrong. The headline claim from custom silicon vendors is compelling. AWS publishes that Inferentia2-based Inf2 instances deliver up to 40% better price-performance for inference versus comparable EC2 instances (AWS Inferentia documentation). Google makes similar performance-per-dollar claims for TPU v5e and its successors on inference workloads (Google Cloud TPU documentation).


Those are vendor claims, and they're conditional on three things:


**Model fit.** Custom accelerators perform best on well-supported architectures. If you're running a mainstream transformer through a standard serving stack, the economics hold. If you're running something unusual, quantised in a non-standard way, or dependent on a specific CUDA kernel, you'll spend engineering time closing the gap — and engineering time in Singapore or Sydney is not cheap.


**Utilisation.** Price-performance advantages assume you keep the silicon busy. A reserved custom-silicon fleet at 25% utilisation is more expensive than on-demand GPUs. Most APAC-facing workloads have sharp diurnal peaks across multiple time zones, which actually helps — a Hong Kong, Mumbai and Sydney traffic blend flattens the curve better than a single-market load.


**Portability cost.** Moving off NVIDIA means moving off the broadest tooling base in the industry. MLCommons' MLPerf Inference benchmarks remain the only credible apples-to-apples comparison, and the submission list there tells you which combinations are actually production-ready versus which exist on a slide.


The practical approach we've seen work: model the unit economics before the architecture debate. A back-of-envelope calculation beats three weeks of vendor meetings.


```text
1  # Cost per million output tokens, self-hosted     2   # Plug in your own numbers from cloud pricing pages     3
4  hourly_instance_cost   =     12.00          # USD, accelerator instance     5  tokens_per_second   =     2400              # measured, batched, your model     6  utilisation   =     0.55                    # realistic, not peak     7
8  effective_tps   =   tokens_per_second   *   utilisation    9  tokens_per_hour   =   effective_tps   *     3600     10  cost_per_m_tokens   =     (  hourly_instance_cost   /   tokens_per_hour  )     *     1_000_000     11
12   print  (  f"USD   {  cost_per_m_tokens  :  .2f  }   per 1M tokens"  )     13   # Compare against API list price for the same model class.     14   # If self-hosting isn't 3-4x cheaper, the ops overhead rarely pays.
```


Run that against both GPU and custom-silicon pricing in your target region. Then add power. In markets where industrial electricity runs materially above the regional median — Singapore and Hong Kong both sit at the higher end of APAC tariffs per published utility schedules — energy becomes a visible share of serving cost, not a rounding error.


## Deployment patterns in the region split three ways


From what we see working with operators across Greater China and Southeast Asia, inference deployment in APAC falls into three patterns:


### Pattern one: API-first, no silicon decision at all


The majority of mid-market companies. You call a hosted model endpoint, you pay per token, you never think about chips. Fastest to deploy, highest marginal cost at scale, and the pattern that breaks first when volume grows. The trigger point is usually when monthly API spend crosses the cost of one engineer.


### Pattern two: Regional self-hosting for data residency


Driven by regulation rather than economics. Financial services in Hong Kong and Singapore, healthcare in Australia, and anyone handling PIPL-scoped data in mainland China. Here the chip choice is constrained by what's actually available in-region — which, for mainland deployments, means domestic accelerators from Huawei, Cambricon and others rather than the latest NVIDIA parts, given US export controls.


### Pattern three: Edge inference at the point of transaction


The most underrated. Retail, logistics and manufacturing across APAC are pushing small models onto devices and on-prem boxes — vision models for shelf compliance, demand forecasting at the store level, quality inspection on the line. Qualcomm, MediaTek and NXP are the volume suppliers here, not NVIDIA.


One engagement shape worth describing: a multi-market retail-services operator running stores across several APAC territories evaluated centralised GPU inference against on-prem edge boxes for in-store vision workloads. The decision came down to bandwidth cost and store-level network reliability rather than chip price. Where connectivity was inconsistent, edge won regardless of the silicon economics. That's the kind of constraint that never shows up in a market forecast PDF.

## Which country is No. 1 in semiconductors depends entirely on what you measure


This question dominates search results and the answer is genuinely four different answers:


- **By leading-edge foundry capacity:** Taiwan, by a wide margin (TrendForce).
- **By memory revenue, including HBM:** South Korea (TrendForce, company filings).
- **By semiconductor company revenue and design IP:** the United States, where SIA data puts US-headquartered firms at roughly half of global semiconductor sales.
- **By equipment:** the Netherlands and Japan hold chokepoints — ASML on EUV lithography, Tokyo Electron and others across deposition and etch.


No single country controls the stack. That interdependence is the actual story, and it's why export controls ripple so quickly through APAC supply chains and reshape AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC on short notice.


## China's chipmaking gap is narrowing at the trailing edge and holding at the leading edge


The honest read: SMIC has demonstrated 7nm-class production without EUV lithography, which is further than many analysts expected in 2022. But yield economics at that node without EUV are poor, and scaling to 5nm and below through multi-patterning gets exponentially harder.


Where China is not behind: mature-node capacity. SEMI's World Fab Forecast has consistently shown China adding the largest share of new global fab capacity, concentrated at trailing edge nodes used in automotive, industrial and consumer devices. For inference specifically, domestic accelerators are good enough for a large share of production workloads even if they trail the frontier on training.


Practical implication for anyone operating in both China and the rest of APAC: assume two separate inference stacks. Plan the integration layer accordingly.

## Semiconductor jobs are being reshaped, not eliminated


AI is already embedded in fab operations — yield prediction, defect classification, process control. That reduces certain inspection and analysis roles while increasing demand for process engineers who can interpret model output, data engineers who can maintain the pipelines, and technicians for an expanding installed base.


The tighter constraint across APAC is headcount, not surplus. Taiwan, Korea, Japan and Singapore all face engineering talent shortages in semiconductor and data centre operations, and every new fab announcement makes it worse. Japan's Kyushu buildout and Singapore's data centre expansion are both competing for the same regional pool.


That's where the distributed-team argument gets concrete. Operations, data engineering and MLOps functions supporting APAC inference workloads don't need to sit in the most expensive market. Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines have deepening technical benches, and the time zone overlap with Hong Kong, Singapore and Sydney is effectively total.


## Where this goes next


Three things to watch through 2026 and 2027.


First, advanced packaging stays the bottleneck longer than wafer capacity. CoWoS and equivalent capacity constraints have been the gating factor on accelerator supply, and according to SEMI's 2025 World Fab Forecast, packaging capacity additions continue to lag front-end additions through the forecast window.


Second, power procurement becomes a board-level item. The markets that solve industrial power — Malaysia, Japan, parts of Australia and India — capture disproportionate inference deployment regardless of where the chips are fabricated.


Third, the GPU-versus-custom-silicon question stops being binary. Most serious operators will run both: frontier GPUs for anything new or experimental, custom silicon or smaller GPUs for high-volume stable workloads, and edge accelerators at the point of transaction. The skill that matters is routing workloads to the cheapest adequate silicon, not picking a vendor.


AI inference semiconductor demand in APAC will keep growing faster than the region's ability to power it. The companies that win won't be the ones with the best chips — they'll be the ones with the clearest unit economics and the operational discipline to act on them. Same as it's always been in retail, logistics and every other margin-sensitive business: measure the cost per unit, then compete on it.
